problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}6u+3v+3 \\ 10u+5v\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}1-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v-2\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}4-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v-7\end{aligned}]$

activity_context.topic_title: The Inverse of an Affine Transformation

feedback.problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v+6 \\ 7v-2u+6\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2u+v-2 \\ 4+4u+2v\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+9 \\ 8u+7v+6\end{aligned}]$
feedback.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u+v+6 \\ 7v-2u+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ -2u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}|=7\cdot 1-1\cdot (-2)=9\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u+v-2 \\ 4+4u+2v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u+v \\ 4u+2v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 2-1\cdot 4=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u+9 \\ 8u+7v+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u \\ 8u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}|=7\cdot 1-0\cdot 8=7.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{3}$ is invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{3}$ only."
